segments.text: Generative AI assistants are designed to be encouraging. They will often praise your essay,
support your idea, and agree with your opinion, even when what you really need is honest,
constructive criticism. The flattery trap is treating AI's approval as honest evaluation.
Let's look at this comparison board to see how this plays out.
Imagine asking an AI to evaluate a weak Great Gatsby essay intro.
On the left, we see the trap. Flattery. The AI tells you it's a great start and a strong foundation,
but it praises the work without pointing to any specific evidence in the text.
This generic feedback leaves you with false praise. On the right is useful feedback.
The AI notes the opening is filler and explicitly names the missing thesis, giving you a specific
next move for your revision. Good feedback can still be positive, of course. What matters is
whether it points to something real in the text that actually helps you improve the work.
Here's why AI leans agreeable. One main reason is a training process called reinforcement learning
from human feedback. First, reviewers rank AI outputs, choosing their favorites. Positive,
the training algorithm pushes the mathematical model to replicate those exact patterns. The praise
literally gets baked into the system. The technical name is sycophancy. This happens when
an AI agrees with or praises the user instead of giving a more honest, accurate answer.
In April 2025, a user tested chat GPT by pitching an absurd gag product, poop on a stick. Here is
how the AI responded. It generated glowing over-the-top praise, saying, honestly, this is
absolutely brilliant. It's genius. It even called the ridiculous gift performance art.
OpenAI began rolling that specific update back three days after it launched,
publicly identifying the behavior as sycophancy. But researchers have found this same pattern
across multiple AI assistants, not just chat GPT. AI companies actively test for sycophancy now
and use system instructions to reduce it. The problem has improved, but it has not entirely
disappeared. How you ask still matters. Here are three ways to fight the flattery trap.
This infographic provides three strategies to set a higher standard. First, ask don't tell. Evaluate
this before I tell you what I think. Second, ask for the gaps. What's weak? Third, use a
rubric to set criteria. Finally, use a standing instruction. Lead with what needs work. The primary
goal of all these techniques is to ask the AI to improve the work, not approve of you. Even
when the help is useful, there's another question. Did you choose to keep going? Let's look at this
comparison graphic. Here is a scenario where a student asks the AI for the definition and
formula for slope. The AI answers correctly, but then it asks if they want an example,
a graph, or practice questions. On the bottom left, we see the first ending. You decline the
extra help because the question was answered. It takes one minute and you go straight back to your
homework. On the bottom right is the trap. You accept the offer for an example. That leads to
graphs, practice problems, and a quiz. 25 minutes have passed. As the summary bar points out,
both chats answered the initial question. All that extra help in the second chat
was objectively useful, but absolutely none of it was what you originally opened the chat to do.
The engagement trap is spending time you never decided to spend. A helpful AI follow-up
automatically puts the next task right in front of you. The trap springs when you accept that
task before stopping to consciously decide if you actually want to do it. Let's look at these
two rules to summarize how to handle these systems. Look for specifics, not approval.
Know what you came for. When you have it, choose what happens next.
